title: Rapid prototype deck sprint — facilitation cheatsheet
body:
Purpose:
This is a concise facilitator cheat‑sheet for a 3‑hour, deck‑led rapid prototype sprint with a customer. The aim is to leave the room with a concrete deployment proposal, a prioritized technical risks list, and a 2‑week PoC plan (milestones + owners). This doc is intentionally pragmatic: timeboxed exercises, explicit decision points, and slide prompts for the customer-facing deck.

Core outcomes (what success looks like at the end):
- Validated deployment target (Hosted / Dedicated / Private) and constraints documented.
- 3 prioritized technical unknowns with mitigation plan (owner + quick experiments).
- Draft slide deck for follow-up Proposal (10 slides) with required technical appendix notes.
- Agreed next steps and owners for a 2‑week PoC kickoff.

Room setup / logistics (prep):
- Bring the slide deck skeleton (see Slide Outline below) in Google Slides; presenter access granted to customer PM.
- Zoom + shared Google Doc for notes; enable recording if customer agrees.
- Whiteboard or Miro board pre-seeded with: success metrics, constraints, and a risks lane.
- Required attendees: customer PM, 1 engineering decision‑maker, 1 infra/ops contact, Redwood SE, Redwood Solutions Architect.
- Optional: security/compliance contact for regulated workloads.

High-level agenda (3 hours):
- 0:00–0:10 — Welcome + objectives + quick intros (facilitator)
  - Set the frame: timebox, outputs, what we will not solve today.
- 0:10–0:25 — Customer context and success metrics (customer lead)
  - Ask for a 3‑minute elevator on product, then 12 minutes focused on target customers, key KPIs, and constraints (latency/cost/region/compliance).
- 0:25–0:45 — Current architecture + constraints (customer engineering lead)
  - Capture infra diagrams, data flow, PII/sensitivity, and authorization model.
- 0:45–1:10 — Redwood quick mapping: deployment options & tradeoffs (Redwood SE)
  - Walk through Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private with concrete example TCO and latency expectations.
- 1:10–1:25 — Breakout A: Primary success metric & SLO definition (mixed groups)
  - 15 minutes to draft measurable SLOs (latency P95, cost per 1k tokens, availability).
- 1:25–1:55 — Tech deep dive: inference workload characteristics (facilitated Q&A)
  - Sequence length distribution, request rate patterns, burst behaviors, sensitive prefixes.
- 1:55–2:10 — Break
- 2:10–2:40 — Risk mapping and quick experiments (whiteboard + prioritization)
  - Identify unknowns, estimate impact and effort, agree on top 3 experiments for PoC.
- 2:40–2:55 — Proposal sketch: recommended path and PoC scope (facilitator + SE)
  - 15 minute live edit of slide deck outline with customer feedback.
- 2:55–3:00 — Commitments, next steps, and close (capture owners + dates)

Slide Outline (10 slides — minimum viable proposal deck)
- Slide 1: Title + one‑line outcome (e.g., "2‑week PoC: Private deployment to validate 150ms P95 inference at 10 RPS")
  - Speaker note: state timebox and what we will deliver at PoC end.
- Slide 2: Customer context & product brief (use customer language)
  - Speaker note: surface customer success metrics up front to orient decisions.
- Slide 3: Target architecture (diagram) — current vs proposed
  - Speaker note: call out integration points and data flows (ingress, storage, telemetry).
- Slide 4: Deployment options considered & recommendation (hosted/dedicated/private)
  - Speaker note: summarize tradeoffs in a 4‑line table (latency, cost, data control, time to launch).
- Slide 5: PoC scope & acceptance criteria (explicit SLOs + data/traffic to use)
  - Speaker note: anything not in scope should be explicitly listed.
- Slide 6: Top technical unknowns + quick experiments (owner + duration)
  - Speaker note: be conservative — pick experiments that give binary answers.
- Slide 7: Minimal test plan & datasets (sanitized samples, traffic shape)
  - Speaker note: call out data privacy and masking requirements.
- Slide 8: Roles, timeline, and resourcing (2‑week calendar)
  - Speaker note: who does what each day; include support hours needed from customer infra.
- Slide 9: Risks & mitigation (3 highest risks with contingency triggers)
  - Speaker note: include rollback/fallback plan (e.g., degrade to smaller model or route to hosted).
- Slide 10: Ask & next steps (approval, budget, calendar invite to kickoff)
  - Speaker note: propose exact date for PoC kickoff and required approvals.

Facilitation cues & timeboxing tips:
- Micro‑timeboxing: call out remaining time at 7, 3, and 1 minutes.
- Use the red card: if discussion goes off on tangents, park in "parking lot" and refocus on decision needed.
- When debate stalls on subjective tradeoffs, force a quick vote: scale 1–5 and capture rationale.
- Keep engineering deep dives to 30 minutes maximum; convert unresolved infra items into discrete experiments.

Priority risk examples (language to use with customer):
- "Data residency unknowns" — Impact: legal/regulatory. Quick experiment: validate KMS/HSM integration in Private deploy. Owner: customer infra + Redwood SA.
- "Throughput mismatch under burst" — Impact: poor user latency. Quick experiment: synthetic burst test on Dedicated pool at representative sequence lengths. Owner: Redwood SE.
- "Quality regression after quantization" — Impact: UX drop. Experiment: run golden prompt set with float16 vs q4 benchmarks and report metric deltas. Owner: Applied ML.

Artifacts to produce before leaving the call:
- Draft 10‑slide follow‑up deck (populate live) — owner: Redwood SE (draft in shared slides).
- 2‑page PoC statement of work (scope, acceptance, timeline) — owner: solutions-eng PM.
- Risk/experiment tracker (Google Sheet) — owner: customer engineering + Redwood SE.

Roles & responsibilities (recommended):
- Customer PM: final signoff on success metrics + calendar approvals.
- Customer Engineering Lead: provide infra diagrams, short list of sample data, and access to a sandbox.
- Redwood SE (facilitator): runs workshop and drafts proposal slides.
- Redwood Solutions Architect: authors technical appendix and PoC runbooks.
- Applied ML contact: identifies quantization/quality experiments needed.

Post‑workshop follow up template (send within 24 hours):
Subject: Recap + PoC proposal (2‑week sprint) — [Customer Name]
Body bullets to include:
- Thank you + restate outcomes achieved in the session.
- Attach: draft 10‑slide deck, 2‑page PoC SOW, risk tracker link.
- Request: sign‑off on acceptance criteria and confirmation of infra contacts.
- Proposed kickoff: [date] (offer two options).

Preparation checklist for facilitator (24–48 hours before):
- Confirm attendee list and roles; escalate missing decision maker.
- Seed Miro board with SLO template and risk matrix.
- Prepopulate slides with customer name, date, and high‑level hypothesis.
- Share required prework for customer: brief infra diagram, 2 sample prompts, and privacy constraints.

Common failure modes and recovery moves:
- Failure mode: no clear success metrics from customer. Recovery: propose 2 suggested SLOs derived from their stated product KPIs and ask customer to pick.
- Failure mode: security/legal blocks immediate data sharing. Recovery: push for synthetic/sanitized dataset and propose small synthetic traffic generator for PoC.
- Failure mode: customer asks for a large scale proof beyond PoC scope. Recovery: agree to a small experiment to validate the core unknowns, then schedule a follow up to scope ramp.

Notes / facilitator heuristics (keep handy):
- Aim for binary experiments: by the end of week 1 we should have answers to the 3 top unknowns.
- Prioritize experiments that unblock go/no‑go decisions for deployment tier.
- Keep the deck customer‑centric — low technical jargon on early slides, escalate to appendix for deep details.

Parking lot (common items to park):
- Long term cost modeling per million tokens (defer to billing workshop).
- Full security & compliance audit (schedule separate session with security team).
- Multi‑region failover design (defer until post‑PoC scalability review).

End of cheat‑sheet — use this as a one‑page reference during the session. If the session yields major architecture changes, convert the deck appendix into a short technical design doc and loop in platform engineering for capacity estimates.
